title: Roots, mark, and compact (how the GC finds live objects)
hook: The garbage collector starts from roots — stack slots, static fields, and handles — marks everything reachable, then compacts surviving objects so free memory is contiguous.

blocks.text: A garbage collection pass has phases: find roots, mark reachable objects, optionally relocate survivors, and update references. Roots include thread stacks, static fields, interop handles (GCHandle), and the finalizer queue. Unmarked objects are reclaimed. Compaction moves live SOH objects together to reduce fragmentation.

entries.plainDefinition: A starting reference the collector treats as definitely live.
entries.example: A local variable still in scope is a root.

entries.plainDefinition: Traverse the object graph from roots and flag reachable objects.
entries.example: If your cache dictionary is rooted, every value it holds stays live.

entries.plainDefinition: Move surviving objects to eliminate gaps on the SOH.
entries.example: After compacting, bump allocation can reuse one contiguous block.

blocks.text: A Redis connection singleton that still references a huge deserialized object keeps that object alive even if no request uses it anymore. Pinning (fixed, GCHandleType.Pinned) prevents compaction around pinned objects — important for interop. Understanding roots explains mysterious memory growth.

blocks.title: What interviewers want
blocks.body: Describe mark-and-compact from roots. Mention stacks, statics, and handles. Note LOH may not compact every time.

snippet.label: Static root keeps objects alive

snippet.explanation: Pinned objects cannot move during compaction until the handle is freed.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Static caches that never evict entries. Pinning more than necessary and fragmenting the heap. Assuming GC will collect an object still referenced from an event handler closure.

blocks.text: Mark-and-compact is a tracing collector: roots include thread stacks, CPU registers, static fields, GCHandles, and the finalizer queue. The mark phase walks the object graph; sweep frees unreachable objects; compact relocates SOH survivors and updates every interior pointer. Server GC runs concurrent marking on multi-core hosts; workstation GC favors lower pause for UI. Pinning prevents relocation — .NET 5+ moves pins to the POH. How to prove it in production: dotnet-gcdump shows live object graphs; a memory leak with flat request count usually means a hidden root (static cache, event handler, or undisposed handle).

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Miss a root type and you misdiagnose leaks
Large live graphs extend pause time
Finalizable objects survive one extra cycle
Pinning blocks compaction around pinned gaps

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Describing GC as 'reference counting' or claiming cycles are never collected. Strong answer: tracing mark-and-compact from roots; cycles are fine; static/event roots are the usual leak cause.

interviewTakeaways: Mark-and-compact traces from roots (stacks, statics, handles) to find live objects, then compacts SOH survivors.
Pinning blocks compaction for that object; prefer short-lived pins on the POH (.NET 5+).
In Redis cache services, audit static dictionaries and event handlers — they are the usual hidden roots.
60s: Roots are stacks, statics, handles. Mark traces the graph. Compact moves SOH survivors. Pinning blocks move. Cycles are OK — tracing handles them.
Follow-up: how does concurrent GC in server mode change pause characteristics?
commonPitfalls: Describing GC as reference counting — that gets you rejected because CLR uses tracing, not refcounting.
Strong answer: mark-and-compact from roots; cycles collected; leaks are usually hidden roots.
Long-lived static dictionaries holding large values.
Forgetting to Free() a GCHandle — pinned object stays rooted until freed.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS engines also trace from roots. Closures and globals are common hidden roots in Node services.
An event listener closure in Node keeps outer variables alive — same as a C# event handler holding a delegate that captures locals. Both are hidden GC roots.
